Why I wanted all the voices in one place

It built me a casting room. Every voice with its own play button, filters for the mood I’m after, and one button that sets the winner as the voice of my chat.

I asked it a simple question: how many different voices do you have? About 970, it said. I was like, wow, I was not expecting that large a number. And honestly, it was cool that it actually told me, no hedging, just the count, straight from the catalog its voices come from.

The 970

Then I asked what the categories were. Three, it said. Gender, accent, and tone. That is when it hit me. I did not want to hear about them one at a time, three samples today and three more tomorrow. I wanted to see them all in one place, where I could shop for a voice the way you would shop for anything else, by trying it on. So I had it build me a casting room.

Thirty-five of those are accents, from American to Transylvanian. More tones than I can usefully list here, though I tried once and it took a while. The app I had it build puts all of it behind filters and a search box, with a short preview clip on every single voice. Two days of rendering, but now the whole catalog fits in my pocket.

Hear five of them right here

Before I give you the prompt, try the idea. These are five of his actual voices, each saying its own name so you can tell them apart. Short clips, labeled, exactly as they sound.

This is what 970 voices feels like.

Aria — warm

That’s the whole experience in miniature. Now imagine that times 970, with filters to narrow it down.

The part I didn’t expect

When I started this, I had bigger plans for these voices: content, projects, things that turn into products. Then I read the terms. Some of these voices sound genuinely human, and that stung a little. Warm, conversational, the kind of voice that’s hard to find in AI. And now I get to tell you the part that saved me a lot of wasted time.

Meta’s terms give you ownership of your prompts, not your outputs. The voices stay Meta’s property. The terms don’t ban you from using them commercially outright, but they don’t grant you the right either. All the responsibility for how you use them sits with you. So here’s how I think about it now: the voices are free to explore, but I won’t build my business on borrowed ground.

What they’re perfect for is everything before the business part. Auditioning voices to find your sound. Scratch tracks are rough placeholder recordings that hold the timing while you build your video, swapped out for the real voice before anything goes public. And short clips as examples when you’re writing about the tools themselves, like I’m doing here.

Free voices are for finding your sound. Paid voices are for keeping it. I laid out the whole thing in a separate article, where free stops, where paid starts, and the $6 line that settled it for me.

The app is mine alone, but the prompt is yours

My app can’t be downloaded. It’s private to my account. But anyone with Muse can build the same thing, so I’m giving you the prompt I used.

Download the voice picker prompt

Three steps. First, you need Muse. Here’s my invite link if you don’t have it yet. My code is 5SGVC4. Redeem it in Settings within 48 hours of joining and we both get the token bonus. Second, paste the prompt into a chat with your assistant. Third, audition voices until one feels like yours, then set it as your chat voice. The whole thing takes a few minutes of your time and a few minutes of rendering on his end.

And when you’re done auditioning and ready to own a voice outright, your own voice with the commercial rights to publish whatever you make with it, that’s a different article. It’s linked below.

Who this is for

A person like me wants to find out how things work, is not afraid to try things, and holds high expectations without the beatdown when it gets hard.

Have you ever wished you could just hear your options instead of reading about them? That’s what this is.

Sources & verification

I checked Meta’s AI Terms of Service on October 18, 2026, at facebook.com/legal/ai-terms, the terms Meta’s own documentation points to. Users retain rights in their prompts; Meta retains ownership of the AI systems, and the terms assign no ownership of outputs to the user while placing responsibility for their use on the user. I also checked the platform disclosure rules the same week: YouTube asks creators to disclose altered or synthetic content, and Meta asks for labels on realistic-sounding AI audio. The voice count of 970 comes straight from the voice catalog on October 18, 2026. Terms and catalogs change, so confirm what you see on your own screen.
